text: Tomato Early Blight Disease Tomato early blight is a common fungal disease caused by Alternaria solani. It primarily affects tomato plants but can also infect potatoes and other members of the Solanaceae family. Symptoms: Early blight typically starts on the lower, older leaves of the plant. The characteristic symptom is the formation of dark brown to black spots with concentric rings, creating a "target spot" or "bull's eye" pattern. These spots usually appear first on the older leaves and gradually progress upward. As the disease advances, the affected leaves turn yellow, wither, and drop prematurely. In severe cases, early blight can also affect stems and fruit. Stem lesions appear as dark, sunken areas, while fruit lesions develop near the stem end as large, dark, leathery sunken areas. Causes: The fungus Alternaria solani thrives in warm, humid conditions. It survives in infected plant debris in the soil and on seeds. The disease spreads through wind, rain splash, and contaminated tools. Temperatures between 24-29°C (75-85°F) with high humidity or frequent rainfall favor disease development. Plants that are stressed due to poor nutrition, drought, or heavy fruit load are more susceptible. Prevention: 1. Crop rotation: Avoid planting tomatoes or other Solanaceae family crops in the same location for at least 2-3 years. 2. Resistant varieties: Choose tomato varieties with resistance or tolerance to early blight. 3. Proper spacing: Ensure adequate plant spacing for good air circulation. 4. Mulching: Apply organic mulch to prevent soil splash onto lower leaves. 5. Sanitation: Remove and destroy infected plant debris. Do not compost diseased material. 6. Watering: Use drip irrigation or water at the base of plants to keep foliage dry. 7. Nutrition: Maintain proper plant nutrition, especially adequate potassium and calcium levels. Management: 1. Fungicides: Apply preventive fungicides containing chlorothalonil, mancozeb, or copper-based products before symptoms appear. 2. Biological control: Products containing Bacillus subtilis or Trichoderma species can help suppress the disease. 3. Remove infected leaves: Prune and remove infected lower leaves to slow disease spread. 4. Monitor regularly: Scout plants frequently for early symptoms to enable timely intervention. References: - Cornell University Plant Disease Diagnostic Clinic - University of Minnesota Extension - ICAR - Indian Institute of Vegetable Research
